porbos.title: The Year Both Shades Were Gone • Those Who Wrote the Paper • Three Years in the Valley • Who Was in the Valley, Who Was Not • What the Siege Did Not Stop • News of the Termites • Those Who Tore the Paper • The Day the Moon Split in Two

blocks.0: The Year Both Shades Were Gone
blocks.1: In the last dars we saw that after Hamzah and ‘Umar (RA) accepted Islam, the Muslims for the first time prayed with heads held high before the Ka‘bah. For the Quraysh this amounted to admitting defeat.
blocks.2: All they had done so far; beating one or two, laying slaves on the sand, pressing down the weak; nothing worked. The din had crossed the borders of Makkah and gone as far as Abyssinia. Inside Makkah the two hardest men were now Muslims.
blocks.3: The Quraysh understood that piecemeal blows would not work. Now the whole root had to be cut. The root of the Prophet {{1}} was his lineage; Banu Hashim. And the chief of that lineage, Abu Talib, was shielding him. The rule of Arabia was that to lay a hand on anyone one had first to deal with his tribe. As long as Banu Hashim stood beside him, the hands of the Quraysh were tied.
blocks.4: So the Quraysh decided to cut the whole of Banu Hashim off from society. No one would marry them, trade with them, or speak to them; until they handed Muhammad over to be killed.
blocks.5: Today’s dars begins with this siege. It ends with two deaths and the stones of Ta’if. In between will be a siege of three years; three years of hunger, fear and isolation. There will be a paper which the Quraysh hung on the Ka‘bah thinking it sacred, and which the termites ate from the inside. There will be a moon split in two in the sky, which people saw and still said, magic.
blocks.6: One question can be kept with us through the whole dars. When I remember the person who insulted me, what rises first inside; the wish for his harm, or the wish for his good!
blocks.7: The answer to this question the Prophet {{1}} will himself give at the end of the dars; standing on the blood-stained feet at Ta’if.
blocks.9: The seventh year of prophethood, the month of Muharram. The leaders of the Quraysh gathered in one place. Sitting down, a covenant was written; a full page. In it there were three conditions. One, no one would marry into Banu Hashim or Banu al-Muttalib; neither give a daughter nor take one. Two, no one would sell them anything, nor buy anything from them. Three, no one would sit with them, speak to them, or enter their houses.
blocks.10: These three conditions were to last until they handed Muhammad over to the Quraysh to be killed. The paper was written by Mansur ibn ‘Ikrimah. It has come in the Sirah narrations that after writing it his hand went numb.{{1}}
blocks.11: The Quraysh hung the paper inside the Ka‘bah. So that everyone would know it was not merely a political decision; it was a sacred pledge. To break it meant dishonouring the gods. One thing is worth noting here. The Quraysh did not raise a hand against the Prophet {{1}}. They did not seize his property. They did not imprison him. They only stopped food, marriage and speech.
blocks.12: Because they knew that to break a person you need not beat him. It is enough to shut off the air around him. Even today the method is the same. When you take up the din, no one says anything directly. They just stop inviting you, stop asking after you, look at you from the corner of the eye.
blocks.13: Being cast out is also a kind of beating. But there was one side of this beating the Quraysh did not reckon. When people are cast out, those inside come closer to one another. The bond in which the Muslims of Banu Hashim were bound, after spending three years in a valley amid hunger and fear, served them even in the hard days of Madinah.
blocks.14: Oppression sometimes, unknowingly, builds a community.
blocks.16: Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib went up into a narrow valley of Makkah; Shi‘b Abi Talib. Ringed by mountains on three sides, one narrow mouth; once guards were posted, nothing went in or out.
blocks.17: Not everyone in this group was Muslim. Muslim and non-Muslim together, two whole clans. Because for the Quraysh the quarrel was not about din, it was about blood. The clan that gives refuge to Muhammad, that whole clan is an enemy.
blocks.18: Only one did not join this group. Abu Lahab. The very uncle of the Prophet {{1}}. He left the clan and stayed on the side of the Quraysh.{{2}}
blocks.19: The siege lasted about three years. Inside, the food ran out. Dry leaves of trees were boiled and eaten. Old pieces of leather were roasted on the fire, soaked in water and chewed.
blocks.20: Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA) would say later, one night I went out and stepped on a piece of dry leather. I picked it up, washed it, burned it, ground it, mixed it in water and got by on it for three days.{{1}}
blocks.21: At night from outside the valley the crying of children could be heard; the crying of hunger. The people of Makkah heard that crying. Some had tears in their eyes. Then they went back to their warm houses.
blocks.22: When the months of Hajj came the siege eased a little; someone from Banu Hashim could go to the market and buy something. But Abu Lahab would whisper in the ears of the merchants, ask them for a high price. And whatever they want to buy, you go ahead of them and buy it, so that nothing falls into their hands.
blocks.23: When his own nephew, the children of his own clan, were crying for want of food, he was raising prices. Even the tie of blood cannot stand before disbelief; Abu Lahab is the proof. Days inside the valley passed in one way. Waking in the morning, one found nothing in someone’s house. Someone ate one date divided. Someone sat behind a rock and quietly listened to the Qur’an.
blocks.24: At night the Prophet {{1}} would sleep by turns in different corners of the valley; changing places again and again. Abu Talib did not want anyone to lay a hand on his nephew in the darkness of night. Sometimes himself, sometimes his own sons, he would lay in the bed of the Prophet {{2}}, and move the Prophet {{3}} somewhere else.{{4}}
blocks.25: This man did not believe. But to save his nephew he put even his own son’s life at stake. Khadijah (RA) was then in her sixties. She who all her life had been the richest woman of Makkah was at that age passing her days on boiled leaves. Not a single complaint was heard from her mouth.
blocks.26: Who Was in the Valley, Who Was Not
blocks.27: One thing needs to be made clear here. The siege of Shi‘b Abi Talib was a siege of lineage, not of faith. The Quraysh cast out Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib; because these two clans were giving refuge to the Prophet {{1}}. So all of these two clans went up into the valley; the one who had become Muslim, and the one still a polytheist.
blocks.28: And the weak Companions in Makkah who were of other clans; Bilal, ‘Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab (RA); they were not in the valley. Oppression on them went on separately, in the houses of their masters, at the hands of their own tribes.
blocks.29: That is, in these three years two streams of oppression ran side by side. One inside the valley, laying hunger upon a whole clan. The other in the houses of Makkah, wielding the whip on the weak Companions.
blocks.30: The Quraysh thought, the din is a matter of lineage. Break the lineage and the din will break. They did not understand, Bilal (RA) is not of Banu Hashim at all; yet he is saying ‘Ahad, Ahad’. What has settled in the heart of a person cannot be bound by lineage.
blocks.31: What the Siege Did Not Stop
blocks.32: In these three years one thing, however, did not stop. Da‘wah. In the Hajj season when people came to Makkah from all over Arabia, the Prophet {{1}} would leave the valley and go to Mina, to ‘Ukaz, to the fairs. Moving from tent to tent he called people to the One Allah.
blocks.33: One who is besieged in his own home, hearing the hunger-cries of his own children, watching his wife’s wealth run out; he is calling unknown outsiders to the din. Hardship did not stop the work. The work went on within the hardship.
blocks.34: And inside, some of the Quraysh would quietly send help. Hakim ibn Hizam (RA) would sometimes in the dark of night load wheat on a camel and take it to the mouth of the valley; for his paternal aunt Khadijah (RA).{{1}}
blocks.35: Once Abu Jahl stood blocking the way. A man of the Quraysh named Abu al-Bakhtari then said, he is carrying food for his own paternal aunt; step aside. The quarrel went from words to blows; Abu al-Bakhtari split Abu Jahl’s head with a camel bone.
blocks.36: That is, the Quraysh too were not entirely one. Inside, to many the matter seemed unbearable. When oppression crosses the limit, from within the group of oppressors itself some begin to object. That very objection became one day the beginning of the siege’s breaking.
blocks.38: After three years one day the Prophet {{1}} told his uncle Abu Talib something. He said, uncle, my Lord has informed me; He has sent termites on that covenant. Wherever the name of Allah was written on the paper, only that has remained. All the rest the termites have eaten; the oppression, the severing of ties, the boycott, everything.{{2}}
blocks.39: Abu Talib did not believe. But he had never heard his nephew lie. He stood up. He went straight to the assembly of the Quraysh. He said, my nephew says that Allah has sent termites on that paper of yours. Take the paper down from the Ka‘bah and open it and see. If he has lied, I will no longer shield him; I will hand him over to you. And if he speaks the truth, you will stop this injustice.
blocks.40: The Quraysh agreed. Their thinking was, this time Muhammad would be caught. It was settled that the next morning in the courtyard of the Ka‘bah, before everyone, the paper would be taken down and opened. That very night another group inside the Quraysh was, entirely separately, making a decision of its own.
blocks.42: Inside the Quraysh there were a few to whom this siege had seemed shameful from the start. One of them was Hisham ibn ‘Amr. In the darkness of night he would load food on a camel and take it to the mouth of the valley, then whip the camel and send it running inward.
blocks.43: Hisham went and spoke with Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah. Zuhayr’s mother was a daughter of Banu Hashim; ‘Atikah bint ‘Abd al-Muttalib. He said, Zuhayr, you eat your fill, wear fine clothes, marry; and your own maternal uncles are starving to death in the valley. By Allah, if Abu Jahl’s own maternal uncles were there, he would never have agreed to this paper.
blocks.44: Zuhayr said, what can I do alone! Hisham said, I am with you. After that, one by one, joined Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi, Abu al-Bakhtari, and Zam‘ah ibn al-Aswad. The five of them, sitting at night, decided that the next day in the courtyard of the Ka‘bah they would openly oppose the covenant.{{1}}
blocks.45: The next morning, on the very day the paper was to be taken down as Abu Talib had said, Zuhayr circled the Ka‘bah, then raised his voice and said, O people of Makkah! Shall we eat well and dress well, while Banu Hashim perish of hunger! By Allah, I will not sit down until this unjust covenant is torn to pieces.
blocks.46: Abu Jahl shouted, a lie! It will not be torn. But one by one five men stood up, each saying, we are with Zuhayr too. The paper was taken down from inside the Ka‘bah. Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi got up and reached out to tear the paper. He saw there was nothing to tear. The termites had already done the work; only the words ‘bismika Allahumma’ were intact, the whole rest of the paper eaten away. Exactly what the Prophet {{1}} had told his uncle.
blocks.47: Some of those who saw this with their own eyes still did not accept. They said, this too is Muhammad’s magic. But the power of the covenant broke. What had been a sacred pledge till then was now a cut-up paper.
blocks.48: That very day the siege ended. After about three years Banu Hashim came out of the valley, thin, weak, destitute; but with faith. The account of the covenant being eaten by termites comes from the books of Sirah; its chain is mursal. It is told in many places as a sign of prophethood, but it is not established by a sound chain. So it can be taken as a scene, not as a proof in creed.
blocks.49: But that the siege broke in just this way; at the hands of the Quraysh’s own men, by tearing the paper; that is clear in several narrations of the Sirah. Allah brought out the voice of justice from within the group of oppressors itself.
blocks.50: The Day the Moon Split in Two
blocks.51: It is reported that around this time the greatest tangible sign of the Sirah occurred. One day a few leaders of the Quraysh came to the Prophet {{1}} and said, if you are truly a prophet, show us a sign. Split the moon in two and show us.
blocks.52: It was night. The moon was full, of the fourteenth. The Prophet {{1}} asked Allah. Before everyone’s eyes the moon split into two pieces. One piece moved to one side of the mountain, the other piece to the other side. In the middle, the mountain of Hira stood clear.
blocks.54: What the Quraysh saw they had no explanation for. Yet they said, Ibn Abi Kabshah has carried his magic as far as the sky. One said, wait, let us ask the caravans coming from outside, did they too see this. The outsiders came and said, yes, we too saw the moon split. Still the Quraysh did not accept.
blocks.57: The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split (into two). And if they see a sign, they turn away and say, this is continuing magic.{{1}}
blocks.58: The word of the verse has not run out even today. ‘If they see a sign, they turn away and say, this is continuing magic.’ For one who does not want to see, even if you show the moon split in two before him, he says, an illusion of the eyes.
blocks.59: Signs never run short. What runs short is the wish to open the eyes and see. Around us too every day how many signs; the birth of a child, a tree from a seed, the unbroken beating of one’s own heart. We pass by. We say, nature.
blocks.60: The event of the splitting of the moon, however, is not some weak narration. It is narrated in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim through several Companions; Anas, Ibn Mas‘ud, Ibn ‘Abbas (RA). Ibn Mas‘ud (RA) said, we were in Mina; I saw with my own eyes the moon split into two pieces.
blocks.61: Before the Hour no such great sign will be seen again. Yet those who did not want to accept did not accept. Signs do not change hearts; hearts are changed by Allah.

footnotes.0: Concerning the covenant of the social and economic boycott by the Quraysh against Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib and its being hung inside the Ka‘bah: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/350–352. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal. As for the specific part ‘the hand of the writer Mansur ibn ‘Ikrimah going numb’, it is only a Sirah narration; it is mursal, acceptable as a scene, not as proof.
footnotes.1: Concerning Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib being besieged in Shi‘b Abi Talib for about three years, the two clans being together irrespective of Muslim and non-Muslim, and Abu Lahab remaining on the side of the Quraysh: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/350–353. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.2: The narration of Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA) concerning the hunger of the siege: Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah. The narration is reported from a Companion; Sa‘d (RA) gave an account of his own hardship.
footnotes.3: Concerning Abu Talib letting his nephew sleep by changing places at night, and, to forestall a possible attempt to kill him, laying himself or his sons in the place of the Prophet {{1}}: Sirah works relying on Ibn Ishaq; Safiyy al-Rahman al-Mubarakfuri, al-Raheeq al-Makhtum. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.4: Concerning Hakim ibn Hizam (RA) secretly delivering food during the siege for his paternal aunt Khadijah (RA): Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.5: Concerning the Prophet’s {{1}} informing Abu Talib that termites had eaten the covenant (except only the name of Allah) and going to verify it: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/375–376. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal. Widely cited as a scene and a sign of prophethood; but not established by a sound chain.
footnotes.6: Concerning the initiative of Hisham ibn ‘Amr, Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah, Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi, Abu al-Bakhtari and Zam‘ah ibn al-Aswad to break the covenant: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/375–377. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.7: The event of the splitting of the moon: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3637, 3868, 3869 and 4864; Sahih Muslim, hadith 2800; via Anas, Ibn Mas‘ud and Ibn ‘Abbas (RA). ✓ Verified. In Sahih al-Bukhari 3868 it is stated that the mountain of Hira was visible between the two pieces of the moon.

quiz.q: When I remember one who insulted me, what does the dars teach?
o: The moment a chance comes, take the equal revenge at once
To raise the wish for his good instead of wishing him harm
To wipe him out of one’s life for ever
To stay silent and nurse hatred inside
quiz.e: At Ta’if, on his blood-stained feet, the Prophet ﷺ asked for guidance for the children of his enemies.

quiz.q: In which year did the Quraysh write the covenant of siege against Banu Hashim?
o: In the seventh year of prophethood
In the fifth year of prophethood
In the ninth year of prophethood
In the eleventh year of prophethood
quiz.e: The covenant was written in the month of Muharram of the seventh year of prophethood.

quiz.q: How many conditions in all did the covenant of the Quraysh have?
o: Two conditions
Three conditions
Four conditions
Five conditions
quiz.e: Marriage stopped, trade stopped, company stopped; these three conditions.

quiz.q: According to the Sirah narration, who wrote the covenant?
o: al-Nadr ibn al-Harith al-Qurashi
‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu‘ayt al-Umawi
Mansur ibn ‘Ikrimah al-‘Abdari
Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi
quiz.e: Mansur ibn ‘Ikrimah; the narration says that afterward his hand went numb.

quiz.q: Why did the Quraysh, instead of laying a hand on the Prophet ﷺ, stop food, marriage and speech?
o: They held bloodshed to be entirely haram
To break a person you need not beat him; it is enough to shut off the air around him
Abu Talib had made the whole Quraysh swear beforehand about this
They were bound to this for the protection of the honour of the Ka‘bah
quiz.e: Being cast out is also a kind of beating; the Quraysh wanted to shut off the air around him.

quiz.q: After taking up the din, people around you keep avoiding you; according to the dars what is this?
o: A sign of weakness in one’s own faith
A clear hint to give up the din altogether
Quite normal, nothing to think about
Being cast out, which is a kind of beating; patience is the way
quiz.e: The Quraysh too wanted to shut off the air around the Prophet ﷺ.

quiz.q: Where did Banu Hashim go during the siege?
o: The cave on Mount Thawr
The valley of Batn Nakhlah
The foot of Jabal al-Nur
Shi‘b Abi Talib
quiz.e: A narrow valley of Makkah, mountains on three sides, one narrow mouth.

quiz.q: Which of the Prophet’s ﷺ uncles left the clan and stayed on the side of the Quraysh?
o: Abu Lahab ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib
Hamzah ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib (RA)
al-‘Abbas ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib
al-Zubayr ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib
quiz.e: Abu Lahab alone did not go to the valley and stayed on the side of the Quraysh.

quiz.q: How many years in all did the siege last?
o: About one year
About three years
About two years
About six years
quiz.e: About three years; after that the covenant was torn up.

quiz.q: Who described his own experience of the hunger of the siege?
o: ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf (RA)
al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi
Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA)
Talhah ibn ‘Ubaydillah (RA)
quiz.e: He would tell of burning dry leather, grinding it, mixing it in water and getting by on it for three days.

quiz.q: Where were the weak Companions of Makkah during the siege?
o: Inside the valley with Banu Hashim
All migrated to Abyssinia together, not one remained in Makkah
In Ta’if under the protection of Thaqif
Outside the valley, in the hands of their own tribes
quiz.e: The siege was based on lineage; the weak Companions were of other tribes, and the oppression on them went on separately.

quiz.q: The siege was lineage-based, yet Bilal’s (RA) steadfastness proves what?
o: Bilal (RA) was in fact one of Banu Hashim
What has settled in the heart cannot be bound by lineage
At that time oppression was only inside the valley
The din is essentially a matter of lineage, blood and tribe
quiz.e: Bilal (RA) is not of Banu Hashim at all, yet he is saying ‘Ahad, Ahad’.

quiz.q: With what did Abu al-Bakhtari split Abu Jahl’s head?
o: With a camel bone
With a wooden staff
With a piece of stone
With the hilt of a sword
quiz.e: When Abu Jahl blocked the way of Hakim ibn Hizam (RA) carrying food secretly for Khadijah (RA), this clash occurred.

quiz.q: What is understood from da‘wah not stopping even within the siege?
o: Da‘wah is the work of easy and safe times only
The Prophet ﷺ did not grasp the gravity of the siege
Hardship does not stop work; work goes on within hardship
Giving da‘wah outside the Hajj season was not permitted
quiz.e: Besieged himself, hearing his children’s crying; yet in the season he comes out and calls.

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ tell Abu Talib had happened to the paper of the covenant?
o: It had burned up entirely in fire
Termites had eaten the paper
All of it had been washed away in rain
Someone had stolen the paper and removed it
quiz.e: Termites have eaten everything; only the name of Allah remains intact.

quiz.q: Who first raised his voice openly in the initiative to tear up the covenant?
o: Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi ibn Nawfal
Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham
Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah
Zam‘ah ibn al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib
quiz.e: Zuhayr circled the Ka‘bah and made the announcement; then four more stood up.

quiz.q: Some from within the Quraysh themselves opposed the siege; what lesson is there?
o: The party of oppressors always stays one, without split
The bond of blood is stronger than the bond of disbelief
The Quraysh secretly loved the Muslims
When oppression crosses the limit, objections arise from the oppressors’ own party
quiz.e: The objection of Zuhayr and Mut‘im became one day the beginning of the siege’s breaking.

quiz.q: Colleagues together are boycotting one person; in the light of the dars what is the right stance?
o: Raise your voice like Zuhayr and Mut‘im against an unjust boycott
Join the boycott with the group
Take no side and just quietly watch the whole affair
Slowly move away from him yourself too
quiz.e: When someone from the oppressors’ own party objects, oppression begins to break.

quiz.q: At the splitting of the moon, which mountain was visible between the two pieces of the moon?
o: Mount Thawr
Mount Uhud
Mount Abu Qubays
Mount Hira
quiz.e: In the narration of Sahih al-Bukhari, the mountain of Hira was visible between the two pieces.

quiz.q: Seeing the splitting of the moon, what did the Quraysh say?
o: This is continuing magic
This is a temporary hiding behind clouds
This is an illusion of our eyes
This is a play of light in the sky
quiz.e: The Qur’an has preserved it: ‘sihrun mustamirr’.

quiz.q: The Quraysh saw the moon in two and still did not believe; what is clear from this?
o: Signs do not run short; the wish to see runs short
The event of the splitting of the moon did not actually happen
Showing a great sign compels people to believe
The Quraysh did not see the sign with their own eyes
quiz.e: For one who does not want to see, even if the moon is split before him he says an illusion of the eyes.

quiz.q: Though signs of Allah are all around, the heart does not respond; according to the dars, what is the direction?
o: Wait for a still greater and clearer sign
Stop thinking about all signs altogether
Try to understand everything by reasoning alone
Ask Allah for the wish to see and softness of heart
quiz.e: Signs do not run short; the wish to see runs short; hearts are changed by Allah.

porbos.title: Abu Talib’s Last Bed • What He Could Not Do • Forty Days Later, Another House • The Year of Sorrow • On the Road to Ta’if • Ten Days of Humiliation

blocks.1: Some time after the siege broke, the tenth year of prophethood. Abu Talib was old, ill. On his deathbed. This man had held the Prophet {{1}} to his chest from the age of eight. He had loved him more than his own sons. Taken him along on journeys, lifted food and fed him. Stood against the whole Quraysh. Stayed three years besieged in the valley, staking his chieftainship and his ties. Yet he did not believe.
blocks.2: The Prophet {{1}} went and sat beside him. He said, uncle, say ‘La ilaha illa Allah’. Just one word; with which I will be able to bear witness for you before Allah.
blocks.3: In the house sat Abu Jahl and ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah too. They said, Abu Talib, in this last age of yours will you give up the religion of ‘Abd al-Muttalib!
blocks.4: The Prophet {{1}} said the same thing again and again. They too said the same thing again and again. In the end the words that came out of Abu Talib’s mouth were: he was on the religion of ‘Abd al-Muttalib. The kalimah he did not say.
blocks.5: From the mouth of the Prophet {{1}} came one thing only; I will ask forgiveness for you, until I am forbidden. In this one scene a great truth of the Sirah is held. The Prophet {{2}} loved people with a real love. His uncle’s death in disbelief made him weep; it gave him no joy. He did not want his uncle to go to Hell. So he tried to the last moment, and wished to make du‘a even after death.
blocks.6: The Prophet {{1}} said, by Allah, until I am forbidden I will keep asking forgiveness for you.{{2}}
blocks.9: (O Prophet!) Surely you cannot guide whom you love; rather Allah guides whom He wills. And He knows best who are the guided.{{1}}
blocks.11: It is not for the Prophet and the believers to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they be relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are people of the Fire.{{1}}
blocks.13: The first verse needs to be read once slowly. ‘You cannot guide whom you love; rather Allah guides whom He wills.’ This is said to the Messenger of Allah. One at whose single recitation the Christian king al-Najashi wept. One at whose one page of Qur’an ‘Umar (RA) went out to kill and came back Muslim.
blocks.14: That very man could not make his own uncle, whom he loved like a father, who had shielded him for forty years, say a single kalimah. Because the work of giving guidance is not the prophet’s. The prophet’s work is to convey. Placing it in the heart is Allah’s.
blocks.15: From here a point for us. Someone at home does not pray, is far from the din; and we, unable to change him, break down. We blame ourselves, think there is a flaw in my effort.
blocks.16: The Prophet {{1}} could not change his uncle. That was no flaw in his effort. Our responsibility is to be beside them, behave well, say the word gently when the chance comes, and make du‘a. To leave the result in Allah’s hands.
blocks.17: The person for whom even the Prophet {{1}} wished to seek forgiveness, even his guidance lay in the end in Allah’s decision. What we can, that much is our work. To torment oneself over the rest is wrong.
blocks.18: What Abu Talib gave the Prophet {{1}} is not little; forty years of refuge, love, standing against the whole Quraysh, a three-year siege. But none of this is a substitute for faith.
blocks.19: Only one thing will be of use in the Hereafter; dying with ‘La ilaha illa Allah’. Relations, favours, lineage; these have value in this world, not on the plain of Qiyamah. The Prophet {{1}} later said, Abu Talib will be in the lightest punishment of Hell; under his two feet two shoes of fire, in which his brain will boil. And he will be the person with the least punishment in Hell.{{2}}
blocks.20: The uncle for whom the Prophet {{1}} did so much, his end too did not change without faith.
blocks.22: Within a couple of months of Abu Talib’s passing, another death. Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA). Twenty-five years of companionship. Mother of six children. The day the Prophet {{1}} came home from the cave of Hira trembling, lay down saying ‘cover me with a cloak’; the first person who believed him that day was this Khadijah (RA). She said, Allah will never humiliate you. You maintain the rights of kin, bear the burden of the helpless, serve the guest.
blocks.23: When the whole of Makkah was calling him a liar, one person at home was saying, I know you are truthful. All her wealth she had poured out on the path of the din; buying and freeing slaves, feeding the poor, the costs of da‘wah. In the three years of the siege that wealth had run out entirely.
blocks.24: Once Jibril (AS) came and told the Prophet {{1}}, give Khadijah (RA) salaams from her Lord and from me. And give her the glad tidings of a palace of pearl in Paradise, where there is no noise, no weariness.{{2}}
blocks.25: Many years after Khadijah’s (RA) death the Prophet {{1}} still remembered her. If someone gave a gift, he would send a share to the houses of Khadijah’s (RA) old friends. When a goat was slaughtered at home he would say, send it to Khadijah’s (RA) friends.
blocks.26: ‘A’ishah (RA) would say, I was never so jealous of any other wife of the Prophet {{1}} as I was on hearing of Khadijah (RA); though I had never seen her.{{2}}
blocks.27: The one who stays beside you in hard times, no one can ever take their place.
blocks.29: These two deaths in the same year. The Sirah has given this year a name; ‘Am al-Huzn. The Year of Sorrow.{{1}}
blocks.30: One shade was the outer; Abu Talib. Because of him the Quraysh could not openly lay a hand on the Prophet {{1}}; with the chief of the clan beside him that would bring war.
blocks.31: The other shade was of the home; Khadijah (RA). The one to whom, after bearing insults outside all day, one could put down the weight of the heart. In one year both moved away.
blocks.32: After that the Quraysh gained courage. A man on the road threw dust on the head of the Prophet {{1}}. He came home in that state. One of his daughters, weeping, washed his head. The Prophet {{2}} said, daughter, do not weep. Allah will protect your father.{{3}}
blocks.33: Such years come in our lives too. When many things break down together; a dear person goes, the job goes, the body collapses, the places of reliance slip away one by one.
blocks.34: At such a time people think, all is finished. The Prophet {{1}} did not stop that year. Seeing the door of Makkah closed he went and knocked at a new door; Ta’if. This hardship of the Prophet {{2}} was no random misfortune.
blocks.35: Once Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA) asked, O Messenger of Allah, on whom does the hardest test fall among people! The Prophet {{1}} said, on the prophets. Then those nearest to them in rank, then those nearest to those. A person is tested according to the measure of his din.{{2}}
blocks.36: The year in which the most hardship came upon the Prophet {{1}} is not a sign of his rank falling; it is rather a sign of high rank. Our reckoning is the opposite. We think, if Allah loves me then life will be easy. The life of the Prophet {{2}} says, exactly the opposite can also be.
blocks.38: The Prophet {{1}} set out toward Ta’if taking Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) with him. This Zayd (RA) is that same Zayd (RA) whom the Prophet {{2}} loved like a son; freed from slavery and kept with him, and Zayd (RA), instead of going back with his own father, chose to stay with the Prophet {{3}}. On the hardest journey the Prophet {{4}} took one who had proved his love.
blocks.39: About sixty miles from Makkah, in the midst of mountains, a green town. Cool weather, gardens of grapes and fruit, the strong tribe of Thaqif. One aim only; if Thaqif accepted the din, or at least gave a safe base from which the work of da‘wah could be carried on.
blocks.40: Thaqif was one of the strongest tribes of Arabia. The fortress of Ta’if, the harvest and the trade routes were in their hands. They had an old rivalry with the Quraysh. The Prophet’s {{1}} reckoning was, if this tribe stands beside him, the siege of Makkah will weaken by itself.
blocks.41: But the leaders of Thaqif reckoned otherwise. They thought, to give refuge to Muhammad means enmity with the whole Quraysh. This risk they would not take. In Ta’if he met three chiefs of Thaqif; three brothers. ‘Abd Yalil, Mas‘ud and Habib.
blocks.42: He called them to the One Allah, spoke of Islam. One said, could Allah not find anyone but you to send! Another said, I swear by the covering of the Ka‘bah, if you are truly the Messenger of Allah then even speaking with you is dangerous for me. The third said, go, return to your own city. We will not say a single word to you.
blocks.44: The three chiefs of Thaqif had turned their faces away on the very first day. Yet the Prophet {{1}} did not leave the town. Ten days he remained in Ta’if. From one group to another, from one gathering to another; wherever anyone was willing to listen, he went and stood.
blocks.45: Not one responded. Instead the chiefs told their people, no one should listen to him. He will not be allowed to stay in our town. After ten days as he was returning, they left no final insult undone. They lined up the town’s riffraff and slaves on both sides of the road. The Prophet {{1}} walked in the middle, and from both sides came abuse, laughter and stones.
blocks.46: They threw stones in such a way that the Prophet {{1}} would be forced to jump aside; and as he moved aside another stone would strike. Zayd (RA) kept bringing his body forward as a shield. His head split and blood flowed. Stone after stone struck the feet of the Prophet {{2}}. Blood gathered inside his shoes, and when he walked his feet stuck.{{3}}
blocks.47: Having crossed a three-day road from Makkah he had come in search of a refuge. He was returning with bleeding feet, empty-handed. Standing on these very bleeding feet, a little later, he made a du‘a in which there was not a single complaint.

footnotes.0: The call of the Prophet {{1}} on Abu Talib’s deathbed ‘say La ilaha illa Allah’, the obstruction of Abu Jahl and ‘Abdullah ibn Abi Umayyah, and Abu Talib dying on the religion of ‘Abd al-Muttalib: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 1360, 3884, 4675 and 4772; Sahih Muslim, hadith 24; via Sa‘id ibn al-Musayyib from his father. ✓ Verified.
footnotes.3: Concerning Abu Talib’s lightest punishment in Hell (shoes of fire under the feet, in which the brain boils): Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3885, 6564 and 6208; Sahih Muslim, hadith 210; via Ibn ‘Abbas and Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (RA). ✓ Verified.
footnotes.4: Jibril’s (AS) conveying of salaams to Khadijah (RA) and the glad tidings of a palace of ‘qasab’ (pearl) in Paradise: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3820 and 7497; Sahih Muslim, hadith 2432; via Abu Hurayrah (RA). ✓ Verified. That Khadijah (RA) is among the best women of Paradise comes in Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3432.
footnotes.5: The remembering of Khadijah (RA) by the Prophet {{1}} even after her death, sending gifts to her friends, and the statement of ‘A’ishah (RA): Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3816 and 3818; Sahih Muslim, hadith 2435; via ‘A’ishah (RA). ✓ Verified.
footnotes.6: Concerning the passing of Abu Talib and Khadijah (RA) in the same year (the tenth year of prophethood, about three years before the Hijrah) and this year being called ‘Am al-Huzn: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. There is variation in the reports on the gap of time between the two deaths (from a few days to a few months).
footnotes.7: The Quraysh gaining courage after the death of Abu Talib, and the incident of dust being thrown on the head of the Prophet {{1}} on the road: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.8: Concerning the hardest test falling on the prophets: Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi, hadith 2398; Sunan Ibn Majah, hadith 4023; via Sa‘d ibn Abi Waqqas (RA). Al-Tirmidhi said the hadith is hasan sahih. ✓ Verified.
footnotes.9: Concerning the journey to Ta’if, the rejection by the three chiefs of Thaqif, the ten-day stay, and the stoning by riffraff as he left the town and the wounding of Zayd ibn Harithah (RA): Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/419–420. This detailed part is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal. The rejection at Ta’if and its hardship are also established by a sound chain (Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3231).

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ ask Abu Talib to say on his deathbed?
o: Subhan Allahi wa bihamdihi
La ilaha illa Allah
Allahu akbar kabira
Astaghfiru Allah al-‘Azim
quiz.e: One word, with which I could bear witness for you.

quiz.q: Which two verses were revealed in the matter of Abu Talib?
o: Surah al-Duha 3 and Surah al-Inshirah 1
Surah al-Qalam 4 and Surah al-Muzzammil 5
Surah al-Qasas 56 and Surah al-Tawbah 113
Surah al-Ahzab 45 and Surah al-Fath 28
quiz.e: ‘You cannot guide whom you love’ and the prohibition of asking forgiveness for a polytheist.

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ later report about Abu Talib?
o: His final account would be postponed
He would be in the lowest level of Paradise, without any punishment
Nothing was told about him
He would be in the lightest punishment of Hell
quiz.e: Shoes of fire under the feet in which the brain boils; yet he is the person with the least punishment.

quiz.q: The Prophet ﷺ could not make his uncle say the kalimah; what is the main reason?
o: The Prophet ﷺ did not try with enough sincerity
The work of giving guidance is not the prophet’s, but Allah’s
Abu Talib was not in a state to understand
Time to make him say the kalimah was not found
quiz.e: Surah al-Qasas 56; the prophet’s work is to convey, placing it in the heart is Allah’s.

quiz.q: Someone at home is far from the din; according to the dars what should we do?
o: Change him by force if need be
Cut off all ties with him
Be beside him, speak gently and make du‘a; the result is in Allah’s hands
Stop raising matters of the din before him altogether
quiz.e: The Prophet’s ﷺ not being able to change his uncle was no flaw in his effort.

quiz.q: Why did Abu Talib’s forty years of refuge not avail in the final judgement?
o: He had not in fact given refuge to the Prophet ﷺ
The Prophet ﷺ made no du‘a for him
In the end the Quraysh no longer recognised the refuge he gave
The worth of relations and favours is in this world, not on the plain of Qiyamah
quiz.e: In the Hereafter what will avail is dying with ‘La ilaha illa Allah’.

quiz.q: A member of the family has given up prayer; what is the first thing to do according to this dars?
o: Slowly reduce ties with him
Shame him before everyone
Stop talking about the din with him altogether
Stay beside him, behave well and keep up du‘a
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ tried and made du‘a for his uncle to the end.

quiz.q: Despite much explaining, someone is not returning to the din; what to do?
o: The work is as much as I can, the rest is in Allah’s hands
Blame one’s own effort and break down completely inside
Abandon his company for ever
Force him back if need be
quiz.e: Even the Prophet ﷺ could not change his uncle; that was no flaw in his effort.

quiz.q: How long after Abu Talib’s death did Khadijah (RA) pass away?
o: Within about two months
On exactly the same day
About a year later
About three years later, close to the Hijrah
quiz.e: In the same year, with a gap of about two months.

quiz.q: What did Jibril (AS) give Khadijah (RA) glad tidings of in Paradise?
o: A golden throne
A palace of pearl
A shaded orchard of fruit
A flowing clear spring
quiz.e: A palace of pearl in which there is no noise, no weariness.

quiz.q: Why could no one take Khadijah’s (RA) place?
o: The one who stays beside you in hard times, no one can take their place
She was the richest woman of Makkah
She was the eldest in age among the wives of the Prophet ﷺ
She was the mother of the first children of the Prophet ﷺ
quiz.e: When the whole of Makkah was calling him a liar, one at home was saying, you are truthful.

quiz.q: A dear one has died; many years later what is in keeping with the Sunnah?
o: To slowly stop mentioning them and forget all
To make du‘a only on the day of their death
To stop taking their name altogether
To remember them and look after their loved ones
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ sent gifts to the friends of Khadijah (RA) year after year.

quiz.q: By what name is the year of these two deaths called in the Sirah?
o: ‘Am al-Fil
‘Am al-Wufud
‘Am al-Huzn
‘Am al-Jama‘ah
quiz.e: The Year of Sorrow; both shades, outer and inner, moved away in one year.

quiz.q: What reality of life is recognised from the ‘Year of Sorrow’?
o: The life of Allah’s beloved servant is always easy
Even when many supports go at once, stopping is not an option
In a great calamity, suspending da‘wah is the rule
When grieved, complaining to Allah is natural
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ did not stop that year; seeing a closed door he went to Ta’if.

quiz.q: The hardest test falls on the prophets; what does this mean?
o: Falling into a test means rank diminishing
The prophets suffered because they sinned
Greater hardship can be a sign of higher rank
Any hardship at all is proof of Allah’s displeasure
quiz.e: A person is tested according to the measure of his din.

quiz.q: Many troubles have come together; according to the dars what should not be done?
o: Remaining patient in the situation
Seeking a new path for the work
Stopping and thinking ‘all is finished’
Seeking Allah’s refuge and help
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ did not stop even in the year of sorrow; he knocked at a new door.

quiz.q: Life is getting hard; according to the dars what could this be a hint of?
o: A test according to rank and measure of din
Allah has become displeased with the servant
There must surely be some big deficiency in the servant’s faith
The servant’s du‘as are not being accepted
quiz.e: The hardest test is on the prophets, then those nearest.

quiz.q: Whom did the Prophet ﷺ take with him on the journey to Ta’if?
o: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah (RA)
‘Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA)
‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan (RA)
Zayd ibn Harithah (RA)
quiz.e: The one who chose to stay with the Prophet ﷺ rather than return with his father.

quiz.q: The leaders of which tribe did the Prophet ﷺ call in Ta’if?
o: The tribe of Thaqif
The tribe of Hawazin
The tribe of Khuza‘ah
The tribe of Banu ‘Amir
quiz.e: Three brother chiefs of Thaqif; ‘Abd Yalil, Mas‘ud and Habib.

quiz.q: What is hinted at by the Prophet ﷺ taking Zayd (RA) on a hard journey?
o: Zayd (RA) knew the roads of Ta’if well
Zayd (RA) was physically the strongest among the Companions
No other Companion was willing to go
In hard times beside you is the one who has proved his love
quiz.e: Zayd (RA) chose the Prophet ﷺ rather than return with his father.

quiz.q: In choosing a companion for a hard task, what does the dars teach?
o: Take the physically strongest in the group
Take the one who has already proved love and loyalty
Take whoever is nearest
Set out alone, taking no one
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ took Zayd (RA) to Ta’if.

quiz.q: On leaving Ta’if, whom did Thaqif set on the Prophet ﷺ?
o: A group of armed horsemen
The riffraff and slaves of the town
The elder leaders of the tribe
A neighbouring tribe
quiz.e: They lined them up on both sides of the road and threw stones.

quiz.q: Who was wounded in the head while shielding the Prophet ﷺ from the stones?
o: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafah (RA)
‘Uqbah ibn ‘Amir al-Juhani (RA)
Zayd ibn Harithah (RA)
Abu Dujanah Simak ibn Kharashah (RA)
quiz.e: He kept bringing his body forward as a shield; his head split and blood flowed.

quiz.q: Is it right to give up da‘wah after being rejected once?
o: Yes, after one ‘no’ one should stop there
Efforts should be kept up only among one’s own relatives
No, the Prophet ﷺ tried for ten days despite rejection
After rejection one can only make du‘a from afar
quiz.e: At Ta’if, going from one group to another.

porbos.title: In the Vineyard • The Angel of the Mountains • ‘Addas • Those Who Listened at Nakhlah • The Hand That Protected • The House Filled Again • Final Word

blocks.1: Having come quite far from the city, the Prophet {{1}}, weary, sat in the shade of the wall of a vineyard. The garden belonged to ‘Utbah and Shaybah ibn Rabi‘ah; two great enemies of Makkah.
blocks.2: They were just there then. From afar they saw the scene; that man of Makkah, driven from his own city, bloodied by the stones of Ta’if, covered in dust, alone. It has come in the Sirah narration that the Prophet {{1}} sitting there made a du‘a.
blocks.4: O Allah, the weakness of my strength, my helplessness and my lowliness before people; all of it I lay before You. O Most Merciful of those who show mercy, You are the Lord of the weak, You are my Lord. To whom do You leave me! To someone who will treat me harshly! Or to an enemy to whom You have given power over me! If You are not angry with me, then I care for nothing. But the shade of Your safety is much wider for me. I seek refuge in the light of Your face, by which the darkness is made bright and all the affairs of this world and the Hereafter are set right; that Your anger not descend upon me, that Your displeasure not fall upon me. To You is the complaint until You are pleased. There is no way, no power, except with Your help.{{1}}
blocks.5: In the du‘a there is a thing worth noticing. He did not say, make me win. He did not say, punish them. He said, if You are not angry, then nothing else is big to me.
blocks.6: In the weakest moment of life the man’s one and only worry was this; whether Allah was displeased with him. When we fall into hardship we think first, what will people say, how much was the loss, who is to blame. He thought, is my Lord pleased!
blocks.7: The last word of the du‘a is not to be thrown away either. He said, the shade of Your safety is much wider for me. That is, even if people turn their faces away there is a place; with Allah.
blocks.8: Standing beneath the stones of Ta’if, the place where the man went to seek refuge was no tribe, no fortress. That place was du‘a.
blocks.10: Many years later ‘A’ishah (RA) once asked the Prophet {{1}}, has any day been harder on you than the day of Uhud! The Prophet {{2}} said, yes. I suffered much from your people. Among that, the hardest was the day of ‘Aqabah.
blocks.11: That day he presented himself to Ibn ‘Abd Yalil. He did not listen to him. Heartbroken he was returning. At a place called Qarn al-Tha‘alib he stopped for a while.
blocks.12: Raising his head he saw a cloud giving him shade. Inside the cloud was Jibril (AS). Jibril (AS) called out and said, Allah has heard what your people said to you. He has heard also how they answered you. Here is the angel of the mountains; Allah has sent him to you. Whatever you command, he will do.
blocks.13: The angel of the mountains greeted and said, if you wish I will bring the two mountains of Makkah together this moment and crush them. The Prophet {{1}} said, no. He said, rather I hope that Allah will bring out from their lineage children who will worship the One Allah and not associate anything with Him.{{2}}
blocks.14: Those who had drawn blood from his feet, he did not wish their destruction. He wished the guidance of their children. The Qur’an has put his whole identity in one line
blocks.16: And (O Prophet!) We have not sent you except as a mercy for the whole world.{{1}}
blocks.17: A mercy for the whole world. Even for those who threw stones. And this hope was not false. A few years later from that very Ta’if people came into Islam in droves; the tribe of Thaqif came to Madinah and gave the pledge.
blocks.18: The city that stoned the Prophet {{1}} and drove him out, from the minarets of that city today the adhan is called five times a day. What the Prophet {{2}} wished that day, Allah gave exactly that; not their destruction, the guidance of their children.
blocks.19: Before cursing someone in anger it is good to remember this scene. An angel came to the Prophet {{1}} and said, say the word and I will crush them. He said, no.
blocks.21: ‘Utbah and Shaybah saw the Prophet {{1}} sitting from afar. A pull of the tie of blood then stirred in them; enemy or not, he was a man of their own tribe.
blocks.22: They called one of their slaves; named ‘Addas. Giving a plate of grapes they said, take this to that man. ‘Addas took the grapes and placed them before the Prophet {{1}}. Before eating, the Prophet {{2}} said, bismillah. Then he ate.
blocks.23: ‘Addas said in surprise, the people here do not say this. The Prophet {{1}} asked, which country are you from, which religion! He said, I am from Nineveh, a Christian.
blocks.24: The Prophet {{1}} said, the town of that righteous man; Yunus ibn Matta (AS)! ‘Addas was startled. He said, how do you know Yunus (AS)! Here no one even knows his name.
blocks.25: The Prophet {{1}} said, he is my brother. He was a prophet, I too am a prophet. ‘Addas bent down and kissed the head, hands and feet of the Prophet {{2}}; those feet where the blood of the stones of Ta’if still was.{{3}}
blocks.26: ‘Utbah and Shaybah, watching from afar, laughed. When ‘Addas came back they said, what, did that man bewitch you! ‘Addas said, master, there is no better man in the world. He told me something that no one knows except a prophet.
blocks.27: The whole city of Ta’if turned him away, and a slave of that very city recognised him. The truth never returns entirely empty-handed. Where a great door closes, a small window opens.
blocks.28: The feet that ‘Addas bent to kiss, the blood of Ta’if’s stones had not yet dried on them. The same feet; to some of hatred, to some of love. What a person is depends on the eye with which he is seen. The whole tribe of Thaqif saw the Prophet {{1}} as a nuisance. A slave from a far land saw him as a prophet.
blocks.30: On the way back from Ta’if the Prophet {{1}} stayed some days at a place called Nakhlah; between Makkah and Ta’if, about a day and a night’s journey from Makkah. At night he was reciting the Qur’an in prayer. He himself did not notice, but a group of jinn were listening to that recitation.
blocks.31: They listened attentively, then went back to their people and warned them, saying, we have heard a Qur’an that is astonishing.
blocks.33: Say, revelation has been sent to me that a group of the jinn listened to the Qur’an; then they said, we have heard an astonishing Qur’an. It shows the right path; so we have believed in it, and we shall never associate anyone with our Lord.{{1}}
blocks.34: The Prophet {{1}} himself knew nothing of this event. Later Allah informed him of the whole matter through revelation.{{2}}
blocks.35: While people were rejecting him, a group from the unseen world quietly listened to his words and believed. The door that closed at Ta’if opened in a place where he himself had not even looked.
blocks.37: He had to go back to Makkah. But Abu Talib was gone. By the rule of Arabia, entering Makkah without the protection of the chief of one’s own tribe or some influential man was then almost the same as suicide. The Prophet {{1}} stopped outside Makkah near the mountain of Hira. From there he sent a message through a man.
blocks.38: It went to the first; al-Akhnas ibn Shariq. He said, I am only a confederate of Banu Kinanah, no one of the Quraysh will honour my protection. The second; Suhayl ibn ‘Amr. He said, Banu ‘Amir does not give protection to anyone.
blocks.39: The message went to the third; Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi. This is that same Mut‘im who reached out to tear the covenant of the siege. He was a polytheist, he had not believed. Yet he agreed with a single word.
blocks.40: At dawn Mut‘im came out with his own sons and the young men of his tribe, weapons in hand. Taking the Prophet {{1}} in the middle he entered the courtyard of the Ka‘bah. Then standing on a high place he raised his voice and announced, O Quraysh! I have given protection to Muhammad. Let no one lay a hand on him.
blocks.41: The Quraysh said, your protection is honoured. The Prophet {{1}} circled the Ka‘bah in peace, prayed two rak‘ahs, then went home. This scene of entering Makkah is worth pausing over. The one returning to his own city had to return under the armed guard of a polytheist. His own tribe was no longer beside him; Abu Talib was gone.
blocks.42: Yet he returned. He did not stop. He did not leave the work of da‘wah waiting for a refuge; he arranged a refuge and went back to the work.{{1}}
blocks.43: Many years later, when the prisoners of the Battle of Badr were being discussed, the Prophet {{1}} said, if Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi were alive today and spoke for these prisoners, I would release them for his sake without ransom.
blocks.44: One good deed of a polytheist; the Prophet {{1}} remembered it year after year, and publicly expressed his gratitude for it. Whether a kindness is small or great, one must deal justly with the one who does it; even if he is of another religion, even if he is of the enemy side.
blocks.45: This whole episode of returning from Ta’if to Makkah teaches one thing. Even in the darkest times Allah sends some hand or other. Sometimes that hand is a slave’s; ‘Addas. Sometimes a polytheist chief’s; Mut‘im.
blocks.46: Help does not always come from one’s own group, from one’s own people. It comes from the place Allah has arranged.
blocks.48: In this year of sorrow itself another event occurred. After Khadijah’s (RA) death, in the house of the Prophet {{1}} there were small girls. The cooking, looking after them, the housework; all in disarray. A Companion named Khawlah bint Hakim (RA) came to the Prophet {{2}} and said, your house has no one to look after it. The Prophet {{3}} said, what can be done! Khawlah (RA) named a name; Sawdah bint Zam‘ah (RA).
blocks.49: Sawdah (RA) had accepted Islam in the earliest period. She had migrated to Abyssinia with her husband. After returning her husband died; now she was alone, elderly, lonely. The Prophet {{1}} married her.{{2}}
blocks.50: Sawdah (RA) was an affectionate, cheerful person. She took the daughters of the Prophet {{1}} to her heart, and set the house in order again. In the year named the Year of Sorrow, in that very year a broken house stood up again.
blocks.51: When Allah closes one door, He leaves a door open somewhere. If you keep your eyes open you can see it. This year began with two graves; Abu Talib and Khadijah (RA). It ended with a new household.
blocks.52: When Allah takes away He reckons carefully. When He gives back too. Though it is named the Year of Sorrow, that very year proved it; Allah never leaves a servant alone.
blocks.54: In today’s dars we heard of a whole year. The three-year siege, the hunger-cries of children in the valley. Then two deaths in the same year; the shield outside and the solace of the home. Then Ta’if; ten days of rejection, and shoes filled with blood from the stones as he left the city.
blocks.55: It is hard to imagine a worse time in a person’s life. And at exactly that time the offer of destruction came before the Prophet {{1}}. The angel of the mountains said, permit me, I will crush them.
blocks.56: He said, no. I want believing children from their lineage. At the start of the dars I had put a question. When I remember the one who insulted me, what rises first inside!
blocks.57: In the Prophet {{1}}, even in the worst moment, what rose was the wish for their guidance. In the coming dars we shall see where Allah took the Prophet {{2}} right after this darkness; the Isra’ and Mi‘raj.
blocks.58: So take one task from today’s dars.
blocks.60: Though bloodied by the stones of Ta’if, the Prophet {{1}} did not wish destruction; he wished the guidance of the lineage of those who beat him. Today I will ask myself one question: when I think of the one who has hurt me, do I wish him harm, or his good?
blocks.61: Today I will take his name and make du‘a once for his guidance, which from today I will not give up.

footnotes.0: The du‘a of the Prophet {{1}} in the garden of Ta’if, ‘Allahumma ilayka ashku...’, is narrated in the Sirah and Dala’il works through Ibn Ishaq and al-Tabarani (Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah 1/420; the Arabic text according to the printed text of Ibn Hisham); many hadith scholars have called its chain weak. So it is used as a scene and a word of consolation, not as a proof of creed or evidence. However, the rejection at Ta’if and the incident of the angel of the mountains connected with it are established by a sound chain (Sahih al-Bukhari 3231).
footnotes.1: ‘A’ishah’s (RA) question, the coming of Jibril (AS) and the angel of the mountains on the way back from Ta’if, and the words of the Prophet {{1}}, ‘rather I hope that from their lineage will come children who will worship Allah’: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3231; Sahih Muslim, hadith 1795. ✓ Verified.
footnotes.3: Concerning the slave ‘Addas bringing grapes in the garden of Ta’if, the Prophet’s {{1}} saying ‘bismillah’, the conversation about Yunus (AS), and ‘Addas kissing the hands and feet of the Prophet {{2}}: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham, 1/420–421. The narration is of the Sirah works; the chain is mursal.
footnotes.5: Concerning a group of jinn at Nakhlah listening to the recitation of the Prophet {{1}} and believing, and the Prophet {{2}} himself not being aware and learning later through revelation: Surah al-Ahqaf, verses 29–32; Surah al-Jinn, verses 1–15. The incident is narrated in the Sirah works as connected with the return journey from Ta’if (Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham; Sirat al-Mustafa). Another incident of this kind, in which the Prophet {{3}} himself consciously perceived the presence of the jinn in the Fajr prayer, comes in Sahih al-Bukhari hadith 773 (via Ibn ‘Abbas (RA)); there is disagreement among hadith scholars whether it is the same incident or two different incidents.
footnotes.6: Concerning the Prophet’s {{1}} entering Makkah under the protection of Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi after returning from Ta’if: Ibn Ishaq; Sirah Ibn Hisham. The statement of the Prophet {{2}} about Mut‘im concerning the prisoners of Badr comes in Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3139 and 4024 (via Jubayr ibn Mut‘im (RA)).
footnotes.7: Concerning the Prophet’s {{1}} marrying Sawdah bint Zam‘ah (RA) on the proposal of Khawlah bint Hakim (RA) after the passing of Khadijah (RA), and Sawdah’s (RA) early acceptance of Islam and migration to Abyssinia: Ibn Ishaq; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra. Narrated in the Sirah and Tabaqat works.

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ not ask for in the du‘a in the garden of Ta’if?
o: His own victory or the punishment of his enemy
Allah’s pleasure and approval
Allah’s safety and refuge
To lay his own weakness before Allah
quiz.e: He did not say make me win or punish; he said, if You are not angry, nothing is big.

quiz.q: In the weakest moment of life, what was the Prophet’s ﷺ one and only worry?
o: How much he had lost in this event
Whether Allah was displeased with him
What people would now think of him
Who in fact was responsible for this disaster
quiz.e: We think what will people say; he thought, is my Lord pleased!

quiz.q: In hardship, which question should one ask oneself first, like the Prophet ﷺ?
o: In the end exactly how much harm was done to whom
What will people think of me now
Who in fact is responsible for this
Is my Lord displeased with me
quiz.e: In the du‘a at Ta’if this was his one worry.

quiz.q: When no one is beside you in trouble, where is the real refuge, according to the dars?
o: In du‘a and under the shade of Allah’s safety
With influential people within reach
With one’s own tribe and ties of blood
With one’s own saved wealth and power
quiz.e: Beneath the stones of Ta’if, the place where the Prophet ﷺ sought refuge was du‘a.

quiz.q: What proposal did the angel of the mountains make to the Prophet ﷺ?
o: To bring the two mountains together and crush them
To send down excessive rain on Ta’if
To destroy the whole harvest of Thaqif
To take away the sight of the enemies
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said no; rather I hope worshipping children will come from their lineage.

quiz.q: In which verse is the identity of the Prophet ﷺ given in one line?
o: Surah al-Qalam 4 – ‘You are surely of a noble and great character’
Surah al-Anbiya’ 107 – ‘a mercy for the whole world’
Surah al-Ahzab 45 – ‘witness and bearer of glad tidings’
Surah al-Ahzab 46 – ‘a shining lamp’
quiz.e: ‘Wa ma arsalnaka illa rahmatan lil-‘alamin.’

quiz.q: For those who threw stones, what did the Prophet ﷺ wish?
o: The destruction of their whole tribe
The ruin of their wealth
The guidance of their children
Famine to fall on their city
quiz.e: A few years later Thaqif came to Madinah and gave the pledge; the hope was not false.

quiz.q: When someone has done wrong, which scene is good to remember before cursing him?
o: The verse revealed about the destruction of Abu Lahab
The discussion about the prisoners of Badr
The Prophet’s ﷺ saying ‘no’ to the angel’s proposal
The splitting of the moon before the Quraysh
quiz.e: The angel said, say the word and I will crush them; the Prophet ﷺ said, no.

quiz.q: What is the name of the slave who brought grapes in the garden of Ta’if?
o: Salman
Yasar
Suhayb (RA)
‘Addas
quiz.e: A Christian slave of Nineveh; he was surprised when the Prophet ﷺ said ‘bismillah’.

quiz.q: The whole of Ta’if turned him away, one slave recognised him; what truth is in this?
o: The truth in the end always returns empty-handed
Slaves are far more intelligent than tribal leaders
The leaders of tribes are never the sort to believe
Where a great door closes, a small window opens
quiz.e: The truth never returns entirely empty-handed; the faith of ‘Addas is the proof.

quiz.q: On the way back from Ta’if, who at Nakhlah listened to the recitation of the Prophet ﷺ and believed?
o: A group of Bedouin travellers
A group of jinn
A few local farmers of Nakhlah
A few Jewish merchants from far away
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ himself did not notice; later Allah informed him through revelation (Surah al-Jinn 1–2).

quiz.q: Returning from Ta’if, under whose protection did the Prophet ﷺ finally enter Makkah?
o: al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi
Suhayl ibn ‘Amr al-‘Amiri
Mut‘im ibn ‘Adi ibn Nawfal
al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah al-Makhzumi
quiz.e: The first two refused; Mut‘im, a polytheist, agreed with a single word.

quiz.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ say about Mut‘im concerning the prisoners of Badr?
o: Had he been alive I would have taken his sons prisoner along with these
Had he been alive I would not have raised his name again
Had he been alive I would have taken his sons prisoner
Had he been alive I would have released them without ransom
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ remembered one good deed of a polytheist year after year.

quiz.q: What courtesy is learned from the Prophet ﷺ remembering Mut‘im’s kindness?
o: One must deal justly with the doer of kindness, even if from the enemy side
Only kindnesses done by Muslims are to be remembered
Responsibility ends once one returns one kindness for a kindness
Taking kindness from a polytheist is not right at all
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ openly expressed his gratitude to him year after year.

quiz.q: The Prophet ﷺ arranged a refuge to enter Makkah; what side of him shows here?
o: Fearing the Quraysh he had drawn back from da‘wah altogether
He wished to leave Makkah for good
He did not leave da‘wah waiting for a refuge, he arranged and returned to the work
He had reached a compromise with the Quraysh
quiz.e: His own tribe no longer beside him, yet he returned, he did not stop.

quiz.q: What to do when an opponent does a kindness?
o: Deny the kindness he did
Deal justly with him and express gratitude
Say nothing and stay silent
Suspect him by looking for a hidden motive behind the kindness
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ remembered the kindness of the polytheist Mut‘im year after year.

quiz.q: When your own house or group is not helping, what does the dars say?
o: One should give up the hope of help altogether
The hope of help can be kept only with one’s own blood relatives
Help comes from the place Allah arranges, and it may not be from one’s own group
It is better to fight on alone, looking at no one
quiz.e: The Prophet’s ﷺ help came from a slave and a polytheist chief.

quiz.q: After Khadijah (RA), who made the proposal for the Prophet’s ﷺ household?
o: Khawlah bint Hakim (RA)
Umm Ayman Barakah (RA)
Fatimah bint Asad (RA)
Umm al-Fadl Lubabah (RA)
quiz.e: Khawlah (RA) made the proposal and named Sawdah bint Zam‘ah (RA).

quiz.q: The great doors of opportunity are closing one by one; what should be remembered according to the dars?
o: Now there is nothing more to do, all is finished
When Allah closes one door, He leaves one open somewhere
There must certainly be some big shortfall in my own ability
There is no way but to sit quietly and wait
quiz.e: Makkah closed, Ta’if turned away; yet the faith of ‘Addas and the protection of Mut‘im opened.
